newsitem.title: MEXICO: Spanglish controversy rages at language conference.
newsitem.headline: Spanglish controversy rages at language conference.

text.p: For millions of Spanish-speakers, "faxear" is to send a fax, shifting gears is done by stepping on the "clotch" and you wear a "smoking" to attend a formal party.

For Angel Martin Municio, vice director of the Royal Spanish Academy that determines what is and what is not Spanish, such inventions are an affront to the language that merely reflect the speaker's lack of education.
"Nonsense," says Juan Bruce Novoa, a Spanish literature professor at the University of California Irvine, for whom derivations from "Spanglish" add vitality to an evolving language.

The debate over Spanglish was one of the undercurrents in this old Mexican mining town during the First International Congress on the Spanish Language, a meeting of hundreds of experts seeking to analyse and perfect the primary langauage for 20 countries and nearly 400 million people.
"You can't just let people say whatever they like," Municio told Reuters. "This 'faxear' is simply a lack of care, poor linguistic education. It's like a suit full of spots."

Yet mixing English and Spanish is a way of life in much of the United States, where millions of Hispanics have been forced to assimilate, as well as in Latin America, which is bombarded with Hollywood movies and U.S.-made products.

In southern Texas, they call their particular lexicon Tex-Mex, the same term used for the local food and music. It is a sort of linguistic dance from one language to the other, often switching in mid-sentence.
In many parts of the Mexican border town of Tijuana there is more English spoken on the streets than in some neighbourhoods of Los Angeles two hours up the road.
In New York it is even more confusing with Puerto Ricans, Dominicans and Mexicans mixing up the languages.
With the advent of the Internet and computer technology, terms like "cliquear", "modem" and "mouse" have become common usage in Spanish.
The jumbling is considered a bastardization of the Spanish language by some purists.

"Well, but bastards are always the most healthy of any family," said Bruce Novoa, a Chicano, or Mexican-American, professor in Southern California. "It's even a literary motif. Those who were not product of the legitimate line are usually the ones who were the most innovative."

Those who cringe at the sound of a Mexican gardener in the United States saying he will hop in his "trocka" to go to work in somebody's "yarda" should consider that much of formal, modern-day English and Spanish has foreign roots, he said.

"Spanish is the wonderful creation of a series of bastardizations of frontier languagues," Bruce Novoa said, noting Arabic, Celtic and English influences in past centuries as well as local languages in the Basque, Catalan and Galicia regions of Spain.
"It shouldn't be seen as a threat," he said. "This all brings vitality to the language."
